title: Darwin's three-ingredient recipe
text: Darwin's argument needs three things. Individuals vary. Much of that variation is inherited. Far more are born than survive. So helpful traits spread. That's natural selection.
author: Charles Darwin
source: On the Origin of Species, ch. 4 (1859)
more:
None of the three was controversial on its own. Breeders knew animals vary and pass traits on, and Thomas Malthus had written about populations outgrowing their food. Darwin, and independently Alfred Russel Wallace, saw what happens when all three act over immense spans of time. Their ideas were first presented together in 1858.

No goal or designer is needed. Selection filters each generation, keeping what works a bit better there and then. This thread goes step by step.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

text: …the slowest breeder of all known animals … at the end of the fifth century there would be alive fifteen million elephants, descended from the first pair.
author: Charles Darwin
source: On the Origin of Species, ch. 3 (1859)
more:
This is the pressure behind natural selection. Every species can multiply faster than its world can support. Darwin chose the elephant on purpose, the slowest breeder he knew. In later editions he redid the sums and got nearly nineteen million elephants after about 750 years.

Elephant numbers don't actually explode, so most young of every species must die before breeding. Darwin called this the struggle for existence. Any small inherited edge changes who gets to be a parent.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

title: Soot turned the moths black
text: Peppered moths are usually pale, blending into lichen-covered bark. Then Industrial Revolution soot blackened England's trees. By 1895, 98 percent of moths recorded near Manchester were dark.
source: Wikipedia: Peppered moth evolution
more:
Birds hunt moths by sight. On pale bark, dark moths got eaten. On sooty bark, pale ones did. After clean-air laws took effect, the pale form came back. That's natural selection, visible within a human lifetime.

Bernard Kettlewell studied this between 1953 and 1956, and his work was later attacked, even accused of fraud. The geneticist Michael Majerus then ran a careful seven-year study starting in 2001, published after his death in 2012. It backed Kettlewell in detail.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

title: Darwin's finches, caught evolving
text: On the Galápagos island of Daphne Major, a 1977 drought left mostly big, tough seeds. Many finches died. The next generation had measurably larger beaks.
source: Wikipedia: Peter and Rosemary Grant; Darwin's finches
more:
Peter and Rosemary Grant have studied the finches there since 1973, catching, measuring and blood-sampling them for six months of every year. Darwin assumed selection was too slow to watch. In the 1977 rainy season only 24 millimetres of rain fell, so small soft seeds ran out and birds that could crack hard ones survived.

It can run the other way too. After a 2003 drought, with a bigger rival finch species on the island, the medium ground finch's average beak got smaller.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

title: Whales once walked on land
text: About 50 million years ago, in what is now South Asia, wolf-like animals such as Pakicetus lived around water. Their descendants became whales. Whales' closest living relatives are hippos.
source: Wikipedia: Evolution of cetaceans; Pakicetus
more:
Whale evolution is one of the best-documented changes in the fossil record. It runs from Pakicetus at the water's edge, through Ambulocetus, whose name means walking whale, to fully marine forms with shrunken hind limbs.

Many living whales still carry small pelvic bones deep inside the body. Gene studies, independent of the fossils, put whales among the even-toed hoofed mammals, sharing an ancestor with hippos around 55 million years ago.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

title: One code for all life
text: Bacteria, mushrooms, oak trees and you read DNA with nearly the same code: 64 three-letter codons. So engineered bacteria have made human insulin for medicine since 1982.
source: Wikipedia: Genetic code; Insulin (medication)
more:
Nothing forced the code to be this way. Francis Crick suggested it may be a frozen accident, fixed early and then locked in, because changing it would scramble almost every protein a cell makes. That nearly all life shares it is strong evidence of one common ancestor.

Biologists call that ancestor LUCA, the last universal common ancestor. Most studies put it at least 3.5 billion years ago. The finches on Daphne Major and the bacteria in your gut are distant cousins through it.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

text: There is grandeur in this view of life … from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
author: Charles Darwin
source: On the Origin of Species, ch. 14 (1859)
more:
These are the last words of the first edition of the Origin. Look at the end: have been, and are being, evolved. Darwin knew evolution was still happening, as the moths and finches in this thread show.

The thread in one breath: living things vary, much of that is inherited, far more are born than survive, and so the environment keeps editing every species. Given time, that links whales to hippos and you to everything alive.

thread.title: How evolution works, step by step (7 cards)

text: When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe.
author: John Muir
source: My First Summer in the Sierra, ch. 6 (1911)
more:
In 1869 a young John Muir spent a summer in California's Sierra Nevada, working with a flock of sheep being driven to mountain pastures. His journal from those months became this book in 1911.

The line usually gets passed around in looser paraphrases. This is how he actually wrote it, and it's the heart of what we now call ecology. Muir went on to co-found the Sierra Club.

text: Hence, both in space and time, we seem to be brought somewhat near to that great fact—that mystery of mysteries—the first appearance of new beings on this earth.
author: Charles Darwin
source: The Voyage of the Beagle, ch. 17 (2nd ed., 1845)
more:
Darwin wrote this about the Galápagos Islands, which HMS Beagle reached in September 1835. Such young volcanic islands, with lava flows still sharp, held many creatures found nowhere else.

The phrase was borrowed. The astronomer John Herschel used it in an 1836 letter to the geologist Charles Lyell, about how extinct species get replaced by new ones. On the Origin of Species, published 24 years after the visit, was Darwin's answer.

text: Heaven is under our feet as well as over our heads.
author: Henry David Thoreau
source: Walden, ch. 16, The Pond in Winter (1854)
more:
Thoreau wrote this after cutting through a foot of snow and a foot of ice on Walden Pond. Kneeling to drink, he looked down into what he called the quiet parlor of the fishes, lit softly as if through ground glass.

In the same chapter, people claimed the pond was bottomless. So he sounded it with a cod-line and a stone. Its greatest depth was exactly one hundred and two feet.

title: Water bears in open space
text: Dried-out tardigrades spent 10 days riding outside a spacecraft in 2007, exposed to the vacuum of space. Rehydrated back on Earth, they revived and went on laying eggs.
source: Wikipedia: Tardigrade (FOTON-M3 mission)
more:
Tardigrades, or water bears, are tiny eight-legged animals. When the moss or pond they live in dries out, they pull in their legs, lose almost all their water and their metabolism stops. In this state, called a tun, they can wait out conditions that kill nearly anything else.

Vacuum alone had no significant effect on them. Unfiltered solar ultraviolet light killed most, though a few still recovered. On mosses they can reach over 2 million per square metre.

title: A shark born before Darwin
text: Greenland sharks may be the longest-lived vertebrates. Dating their eye lenses suggests at least 272 years. The oldest studied was put at 392 years, give or take 120.
source: Nielsen et al., Science (2016); Wikipedia: Greenland shark
more:
Sharks have no bony parts that lay down yearly rings, so their age was a mystery. In 2016 researchers dated the core of the eye lens, which forms during development and never changes. Its carbon-14, including the spike from bomb tests in the 1950s and 60s, gave each shark's birth date.

They live in the cold North Atlantic and Arctic, grow over 6 metres long and don't mature until around 150. Some alive today were born before Charles Darwin.

title: 2.4 million new cells a second
text: An adult makes about 2.4 million new red blood cells every second. Each lasts roughly 100 to 120 days. At any moment you carry some 20 to 30 trillion.
source: Wikipedia: Red blood cell
more:
They're by far the most numerous cells in your body. As they mature in the bone marrow, they lose their nucleus and most of their machinery to make room for haemoglobin, the iron-rich protein that carries oxygen. With no nucleus they can't divide or repair themselves, so they need constant replacing.

A typical one makes a full lap of your body in about a minute. Over three to four months, that's well over a hundred thousand trips.

title: The ten-to-one bacteria myth
text: A popular claim says your bacteria outnumber your cells ten to one. A 2016 recount found about 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells.
source: Sender, Fuchs and Milo, PLoS Biology and Cell (2016); Wikipedia: Human microbiome
more:
That's for a typical adult man. The ten-to-one figure came from rough estimates in the 1970s that got repeated for decades without being checked. Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo at the Weizmann Institute redid the sums with modern data. Blood cells make up about 90 percent of the human count.

By weight your bacteria come to about 0.2 kilograms. Most live in your gut, where they help digest food and train your immune system.

title: A tree older than the pyramids
text: Methuselah, a Great Basin bristlecone pine, started growing around 2833 BC. It was already centuries old when the Great Pyramid of Giza was finished.
source: Wikipedia: Pinus longaeva
more:
That makes it more than 4,850 years old, credited as the oldest known living non-clonal organism. Bristlecones grow very slowly, high in the cold, dry mountains of the western United States. As an old tree ages, much of it can die back until a narrow strip of bark links the roots to a few living branches.

Some clonal colonies, like aspen groves sharing one root system, may be older. Methuselah is a single tree.

title: Bees give directions by dancing
text: A honeybee back from good flowers does a waggle dance. Its angle from straight up gives the food's direction from the Sun. How long she waggles gives the distance.
source: Wikipedia: Waggle dance; Karl von Frisch
more:
Karl von Frisch, an Austrian scientist, was one of the first to decode this, through years of experiments with marked bees and feeding stations. He shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Inside the dark hive the comb hangs vertically, so straight up stands in for the Sun. A run straight up means fly toward the Sun. A run angled right means fly that angle to the right of it. Other bees follow the dancer, then head out.

title: Your cells hold ancient bacteria
text: Lynn Margulis pushed a once-doubted idea: mitochondria, the power units in your cells, were once free-living bacteria. One cell swallowed another and, instead of digesting it, kept it.
author: Lynn Margulis
source: On the Origin of Mitosing Cells, Journal of Theoretical Biology (1967)
more:
Plant chloroplasts started the same way. The idea, called endosymbiotic theory, was proposed in 1905 and 1910 by the Russian botanist Konstantin Mereschkowski but largely ignored. Margulis revived it in 1967 with microbiological evidence.

Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own small chromosomes, separate from the cell's main DNA, and split in two the way bacteria do. Chloroplasts even share a double membrane with free-living cyanobacteria. It's now standard textbook biology.

title: Evolution from the gene's view
text: Richard Dawkins suggested looking at evolution from the gene's side. Bodies die, genes get copied. Genes that build bodies good at surviving and breeding get copied more.
author: Richard Dawkins
source: The Selfish Gene (1976)
more:
In The Selfish Gene he called organisms vehicles that genes build to get themselves passed on. The word selfish trips people up. Dawkins meant only that the genes around today are the ones that were good at getting copied, with no desires involved.

This helps explain why animals help relatives, who likely carry copies of the same genes. That idea, kin selection, came largely from W. D. Hamilton's work. The book also introduced the word meme.

title: Are you still the same body?
text: Red blood cells last about four months. About a tenth of your fat cells are renewed each year. If enough gets swapped out, are you still you?
source: Wikipedia: Ship of Theseus; Bomb pulse
more:
Only partly, because you aren't replaced evenly. The old puzzle is the Ship of Theseus, rebuilt plank by plank. The idea that your whole body renews every seven years is too simple.

In 2005 Kirsty Spalding and colleagues used carbon-14 from Cold War nuclear tests, locked into DNA as cells formed, to date human cells. Many tissues turn over, but neurons in your cerebral cortex basically don't. They're about as old as you are.

title: Which came first, chicken or egg?
text: Philosophers argued over it for centuries, but evolution gives a clear answer. Before you tap for more: did the first chicken hatch from an egg, or lay one?
source: Wikipedia: Chicken or the egg
more:
The egg, by a long way. Hard-shelled eggs that could be laid on dry land appeared around 312 million years ago, long before any bird existed. Fish and amphibians laid eggs earlier still.

Even counting only chicken eggs, the egg wins. Species change gradually, so at some point two birds that were almost chickens produced an egg holding a bird we'd call a chicken. Its chicken DNA was already in the egg before it hatched.
